passage: Researchers in the Svensson laboratory studied three reversible reactions of early carbohydrate metabolism in extracts of rat liver. Each reaction was allowed to reach equilibrium in a sealed reaction vessel at 37 °C and pH 7.0, after which reactants and products were quantified by HPLC to give the equilibrium constant. In a second set of experiments, intact hepatocytes were rapidly freeze-clamped and the steady-state ratio of products to reactants, known as the mass-action ratio Q, was measured for the same reactions. Comparing Q with Keq indicates how far each reaction sits from equilibrium under physiological conditions, and therefore which steps are likely to be regulated. The investigators used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and expected values of ΔG°′ to be consistent with literature compilations. All reagents were of analytical grade, and each reaction vessel was degassed to avoid oxidation of sulfhydryl groups. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.
table:
Table 1. Equilibrium and mass-action ratios

| Reaction | Keq | Q in hepatocytes |
|---|---|---|
| glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP | 652 | 0.652 |
| fructose-6-phosphate → glucose-6-phosphate | 1.93 | 1.74 |
| dihydroxyacetone phosphate → glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate | 0.0545 | 5.45 |

questions.stem: According to Table 1, which reaction operates closest to equilibrium in hepatocytes?

options.B: Reaction A: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
options.D: None; all three are far from equilibrium

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Q/Keq for Reaction B is 1.74/1.93 = 0.90, close to 1, so it runs near equilibrium. Why the others are wrong: A) Reaction C has Q/Keq = 5.45/0.0545 = 100, far from equilibrium. B) Reaction A has Q/Keq = 0.652/652 = 0.001, far from equilibrium. D) Reaction B is near equilibrium.
questions.trap: Choosing Reaction A because its Keq is the largest, instead of comparing Q with Keq for each reaction.

questions.stem: Which control best confirms that the measured Keq reflects true equilibrium rather than a slow approach?

options.A: Approach equilibrium from both the reactant side and the product side and obtain the same ratio
options.B: Lower the temperature to slow the reaction before quantifying
options.C: Double the enzyme concentration and observe a faster rate
options.D: Measure only product concentration at a single time point

questions.explanation: A true equilibrium ratio is independent of the direction of approach; a path-dependent ratio signals the system has not equilibrated.
questions.trap: Choosing a lower temperature or more enzyme, which change speed but cannot show the same ratio is reached from both directions.

questions.stem: For reaction B (Keq = 1.93), what is ΔG°′ at 310 K, in kJ/mol?
questions.explanation: ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq = −(0.008314 × 310) × ln(1.93) = -1.7 kJ/mol (literature value -1.7 kJ/mol). Using log10 instead of the natural log, or reversing the sign, gives the wrong values.
questions.trap: Using log10 instead of ln (giving -0.7 kJ/mol) or dropping the negative sign in ΔG°′ = −RT ln Keq (giving +1.7).

options.A: ΔG°′ is related to the equilibrium constant but not to the reaction rate
options.B: A reaction with positive ΔG°′ can proceed forward if Q is sufficiently small
options.C: Actual ΔG depends on Q as well as ΔG°′
options.D: A reaction with a negative ΔG°′ always proceeds rapidly in the cell

questions.explanation: Thermodynamics specifies direction, not speed. Rate depends on activation energy and enzyme catalysis.
questions.trap: Assuming a negative ΔG°′ means the reaction is fast; thermodynamics gives direction, not rate.

questions.stem: Which mechanism allows cells to drive reactions with large positive ΔG°′ forward?

options.A: Coupling them to a strongly exergonic step such as ATP hydrolysis
options.B: Removing the catalyst so the reaction is not rate-limited
options.C: Raising the temperature enough to make Keq equal 1
options.D: Increasing the enzyme concentration to lower ΔG°′

questions.explanation: Enzymes do not change ΔG°′. Coupling to ATP hydrolysis (about −30.5 kJ/mol) or keeping Q very low makes the overall ΔG negative.
questions.trap: Believing an enzyme or more enzyme can change ΔG°′; catalysts change rate, not the free energy change.
